text: Aligned with Bloom’s Taxonomy  Laurentius Gusti Ontoseno Panata Yudha , Hapnes Toba ,  Oscar Karnalim , Hendra Bunyamin , and Terutoshi Tada  Abstract This chapter introduces an interactive learning system that uses  OpenAI’s large language model (LLM) to automatically create and evaluate essay- style questions aligned with Bloom’s Taxonomy. The system processes educational  PDFs using term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF)-based keyword  extraction (from unigram to trigram) to connect question content to its source, reduc- ing hallucinations. Semantic evaluation is performed with the ada-002 embedding  model and cosine similarity to assess student answers. When similarity scores fall  below a set threshold, the system provides follow-up questions to support adaptive  learning. The platform supports multiple languages and was tested in a two-phase  study with university students in Japan and Indonesia. Evaluation using the technol- ogy acceptance model (TAM) showed high perceived usefulness (0.991) and ease of  use (0.850), with improved results after system updates. Findings also indicate that  documents in their original language (English) produce more stable and accurate  semantic similarity scores than translated versions, highlighting the limitations of  cross-lingual embeddings in AI-assisted educational assessment. The integration of artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) in higher education is transforming  instructional design, assessment, and personalization, with large language models  (LLMs) playing a pivotal role due to their ability to understand and generate human- like text [ 5]. LLMs utilize natural language processing (NLP) to extract key concepts,  infer semantic relationships, and generate pedagogically aligned questions. While  earlier AI-driven approaches have focused on template-based multiple-choice or  short-answer generation [ 26, 29], they often lack contextual depth and adaptability  to diverse cognitive levels, highlighting the unique potential of LLMs for dynamic,  context-aware educational tasks. To address this, our approach utilizes Bloom’s taxonomy [ 7]—a widely adopted  hierarchical model of learning objectives – to guide the generation of questions across  multiple cognitive levels. At the foundational level, questions test recall (remember- ing) and understanding; at more advanced levels, they prompt learners to analyze,  evaluate, or apply knowledge. Embedding these structures into question genera- tion promotes differentiated instruction, encourages deeper learning, and aligns AI  outputs with educational standards. Beyond question generation, automated assessment is another domain where  LLMs can contribute signiﬁcantly. By generating reference answers directly from  instructional materials and comparing them with student responses using seman- tic similarity (e.g., cosine distance over embedding vectors [ 35]), AI can perform  accurate, scalable, and context-sensitive grading. Unlike traditional keyword-based  scoring systems, semantic evaluation accounts for variations in wording and phrasing,  offering fairer assessments that recognize conceptual equivalence. This approach not  only enhances assessment efﬁciency but also provides real-time, formative feedback  that encourages meta-cognitive reﬂection and critical thinking.

This approach not  only enhances assessment efﬁciency but also provides real-time, formative feedback  that encourages meta-cognitive reﬂection and critical thinking. Our system combines automated question generation and semantic-contextual  grading within a single learning platform, using term frequency-inverse document  frequency (TF-IDF) representation to extract anchor terms from educational PDFs  at unigram to trigram levels, ensuring relevance in context [ 20]. It also supports mul- tilingual interactions. User acceptance is assessed using the technology acceptance  model (TAM) [ 10], focusing on perceived usefulness (PU) and ease of use through  (PEU), evaluated with Japanese and Indonesian university students, highlighting  adaptive interaction and pedagogical alignment. Our study presents the following contributions:  • A novel system that generates Bloom’s Taxonomy-aligned essay questions using  OpenAI’s LLM, anchored with local and global context from TF-IDF-based  keyword extraction.  • Integration of semantic similarity scoring, based on TF-IDF, using OpenAI’s text  embedding ada-002 model to compare student answers with reference responses.  • An adaptive questioning mechanism that provides follow-up prompts if students’  answers do not meet cosine similarity thresholds. 8 An LLM-Based Adaptive Learning System for Automated Essay … 127 • Multilingual implementation and testing in two distinct academic environments  (Japan and Indonesia).  • Empirical validation using TAM, highlighting system usability, perceived beneﬁt,  and cross-cultural applicability. These contributions position our work at the intersection of educational technol- ogy, natural language processing, and pedagogical design, making it one of the ﬁrst  systems to offer an end-to-end solution for context-aware question generation and  semantic grading within a multilingual, web-based learning platform.

This section reviews the state-of-the-art in AI-driven educational technologies, focus-
ing on ﬁve thematic areas: (1) Automated essay scoring, (2) Embeddings and text 
similarity in educational NLP , and (3) TAM in education.

Cosine similarity remains an important method in text analysis and automated essay  scoring (AES), valued for its ability to measure the similarity between student essays  and reference texts regardless of word order. While early AES systems relied on hand- crafted features and traditional classiﬁers [ 4, 34], modern systems like ETS’s e-rater  and IntelliMetric utilize NLP and latent semantic analysis to assess coherence and  argumentation [ 12]. Recent research continues to apply cosine similarity effectively  for comparing essays to manually graded references, supporting more nuanced and  scalable assessment in educational settings. Cosine similarity has gained prominence in AES due to its ability to evaluate  student-generated responses against reference answers semantically. Fauzi et al. [14]  used n-gram and cosine similarity to evaluate short essays, while Lahitani et al.  [19] implemented cosine-based scoring in Indonesian educational contexts. These  models, however, struggle with understanding syntactic variation and contextual  nuance–gaps addressed by transformer-based models such as BERT [ 11]. Overall, cosine similarity, whether using the bag-of-words method or TF-IDF,  has proven effective in developing fast and efﬁcient automatic essay scoring systems. However, further development, such as applying n-grams and considering word order,  can enhance accuracy in essay assessment, particularly in contexts that require a  deeper understanding of sentence structure and meaning. 128 An LLM-Based Adaptive Learning System... The alignment of question generation with Bloom’s Taxonomy has been explored  to enhance instructional design. Alammary et al. [ 1] proposed a modiﬁed TF- IDF method to generate Arabic-language questions categorized by Bloom’s lev- els. Melevsko [25] and Scaria et al. [ 32] demonstrated that taxonomically informed  question generation leads to better learning outcomes.

Melevsko [25] and Scaria et al. [ 32] demonstrated that taxonomically informed  question generation leads to better learning outcomes. Recent work by Muñoz et al. [ 26] introduced grammar-based automatic question  generation systems for compilers education, though not Bloom-aligned. Generative  LLMs, like GPT-3, have begun to bridge this gap by adapting embeddings and prompt  engineering to organize questions according to cognitive level [ 23, 39].

section: 8.2.2 Embeddings and Text Similarity in Educational NLP
text: Embeddings, such as OpenAI’s ada-002, are powerful numerical representations of  text that capture semantic meaning across 1536 dimensions. This enables systems to  understand contextual relationships between words or phrases with high precision. The ada-002 model is not only effective across various NLP tasks but also opti- mized for cost-efﬁciency, making it suitable for resource-constrained educational  settings [ 21]. In automatic assessment and interactive question answering systems, embed- dings like ada-002 support semantic-level evaluation, allowing student answers  to be judged even when phrased differently from the reference. This ﬂexibility  enhances accuracy in grading and enables more responsive feedback. Systems like  those described by Serrano et al. [ 33]a n d P a t e le ta l . [28] show how embed- dings improve retrieval-augmented generation, enabling adaptive and personalized  learning experiences. On the other hand, cosine similarity utilizes TF-IDF, a statistical method for  evaluating a word’s relevance in a document compared to a set of other documents. TF-IDF determines a word’s signiﬁcance using two components [ 30]. The ﬁrst is the  term frequency (TF) which measures how frequently a word appears in a speciﬁc  document relative to the total number of words in that document. The second is  the inverse document frequency (IDF) which assesses the signiﬁcance of a word  throughout the entire collection of documents, assigning greater importance to words  that occur less frequently in other documents.

text: The basic formula for TF-IDF is:  .TF-IDF(t,d,D)= ft,d t ∈d ft ,d ×log N |{d∈D:t∈d}| (8.1)  Where:  t: term  d: document  D: collection of documents (corpus)  . ft,d : frequency of term t in document d 8 An LLM-Based Adaptive Learning System for Automated Essay … 129 N: total number of document in corpus D  .|{d∈D:t∈d}| : number of documents where the term t appears  TF-IDF is commonly used in text analysis, such as keyword extraction, text clas- siﬁcation, and document indexing. In the context of education, TF-IDF enables the  assessment of word relevance in teaching materials, aids in automating question  generation, and supports technology-based learning. For example, Alammary devel- oped a modiﬁed TF-IDF method to extract features from Arabic language assessment  questions according to Bloom’s taxonomy, which improved classiﬁcation accuracy  and relevance [ 1]. Meanwhile, Qaiser and Ali utilized TF-IDF to identify relevant keywords across  different domains from documents. Their research results demonstrated the effec- tiveness of TF-IDF in text data analysis for various applications, such as document  categorization and automatic tagging [ 30]. Cosine similarity remains the metric of  choice for semantic scoring in education due to its efﬁciency and alignment with  human judgments [ 30, 36]. Combining embeddings with cosine similarity allows  systems to move beyond keyword overlap and better approximate instructions [ 31]. The global use of AI in education necessitates robust multilingual support, yet  performance often drops in low-resource languages. Studies by Pesovski et al. [ 29]  and Wang et al. [38] highlight that models like GPT perform optimally in English but  less effectively in other languages. While methods such as training on multilingual  corpora [ 8], cross-lingual embeddings [3], and back-translation [24] offer solutions,  they come with added latency and computational costs.

This motivates the use of  lightweight alternatives like our TF-IDF-based approach, which anchors keyword  contexts locally.

TAM provides a framework to understand how users adopt educational technologies 
by focusing on two main factors: perceived usefulness (PU) and perceived ease of 
use (PEU). PU assesses whether users believe the technology improves their task 
performance, while PEU evaluates how easily the technology can be used without 
frustration. These factors are particularly important for automatic assessment sys-
tems that use TF-IDF and Cosine Similarity, where user acceptance depends on the 
system’s perceived beneﬁts and user-friendliness. 
TAM has been effectively applied in evaluating a range of technologies, including 
learning management systems [13], mobile learning apps [16], and AI-based tutoring 
tools [ 2]. Studies by Chen et al. [ 5] and Dahri et al. [ 9] highlight that adaptability 
and clarity–aligned with PU and PEU–are critical to positive adoption outcomes. By 
applying TAM, developers can enhance both the functionality and user acceptance 
of educational technologies [
10].

Our research methodology includes a LLM-based Learning System development. 
The web system is developed by utilizing the OpenAI API and a prompting technique 
based on a few-shot mechanism. The core of the system lies in the context extraction 
and anchoring. Context extraction is performed by implementing the TF-IDF formula 
and extracting the top-10 uni-, bi-, and trigrams from an uploaded document (details 
in Sects. 
8.3.3 and 8.3.4). 
Each extracted context will be further associated with a Bloom’s level and incor-
porated into the OpenAI prompt to generate a series of questions. The complete 
research methodology can be seen in Fig. 8.1. After the system is populated with a 
series of questions, students can engage in question-and-answer interactions. Each 
interaction will be evaluated with an automated TF-IDF scoring system, on a 0-100 
scale. 
To test the system, we conduct a two-step TAM evaluation. The ﬁrst is using a 
general text with the topic of Generative AI taken from [ 27]. The second step is 
an enhancement phase, which was tested in a real classroom situation, using two 
chapters from a textbook [ 15] as the document source.

Our LLM-based Learning System integrates state-of-the-art technologies to create a 
practical and interactive educational platform. It enhances the teaching and learning 
experience by leveraging web-based architecture, generative AI, and secure data 
management practices [
17]. Figure 8.2 shows the technological architecture involved 
in developing and implementing the LLM-based Learning System. 
Lecturers can upload PDF documents through the Laravel front end, as depicted in 
Fig. 8.2 of the system ﬂow diagram. The backend processes these uploads, securely 
storing PDF data in server storage and logging metadata such as uploader information 
and timestamps in the MySQL database. Students access educational materials and 
assessments through the same Laravel-based front end. The system uses session 
management and authentication mechanisms to ensure secure access. It facilitates 
API-driven communication between the front and back ends for data retrieval and 
performance tracking (see Fig. 
8.2, the ﬁgure is initially published in [ 37]). 
Metadata from uploaded PDFs is stored in a MySQL database. This database 
also manages basic ﬁle information and retrieves data for generating assessments 
and tracking student performance. The stored data is used to generate questions and 
compile performance metrics, which are then presented to students.

Document processing begins by applying TF-IDF vectorization to the uploaded text,  covering unigrams to trigrams. In this study, a machine learning textbook sub-chapter  “Regularized Linear Models”, is used as the baseline document, aligning with the  classroom context [15]. Observations indicate that tetragrams produce very low word  frequencies, nearing zero, and do not meaningfully improve the model’s performance  (see Fig. 8.3). Next, based on the TF-IDF results, the terms are sorted by cosine similarity values  calculated across all uni-, bi-, and trigrams. The top-10 highest values, reﬂecting the  most relevant words or phrases in the document, are selected. These top-10 terms are  then incorporated into the prompt, as described in Table 8.1, to provide context when  generating questions and answers for each document page. This method ensures that  the generated questions are pertinent to the document’s content and uphold strong  semantic ties with the uploaded text. When generating questions from a document, especially in cases of language mis- match (such as an English source document translated into Indonesian for question- answering), the system ﬁrst calculates TF-IDF values from the translated version. It then selects the top-10 uni-, bi-, and trigrams from the original language based  on the highest cosine similarity scores. These n-grams form the foundation for con- text anchoring [ 22], guiding the LLM to focus on the most relevant content. This  approach helps prevent the LLMs from generating outdated or semantically unrelated  responses by limiting the output to contextually grounded terms. Three different context anchoring methods were evaluated to identify the most  effective approach for the model.  1. In the ﬁrst method, we examine the anchors used to generate the prompt by  selecting the best TF-IDF weighted ’nouns’ keywords from the entire document. Each page thus receives a ﬁxed set of global contexts. These nouns–comprising  10 uni-, 10 bi-, and 10 trigrams–are embedded along with the full document text,  and cosine similarity is used to ﬁnd the top-10 best contexts.  2. In the second method, a dynamic anchoring approach is used, with each page  assigned a local set of ’nouns’ keywords based on the computed TF-IDF of that  page. The top-10 uni-, bi-, and trigrams from each page are incorporated into  the page’s text, and cosine similarity identiﬁes the best top-10 contexts.  3. In the third method, no speciﬁc context anchoring is applied. Instead, the GenAI  decides which context to use in the generated questions. However, the prompt  includes the page text and Bloom’s taxonomy templates. 134 An LLM-Based Adaptive Learning System... For the ﬁrst and second methods, the top-10 extracted (uniﬁed) uni-, bi, and  trigrams are then used as the context anchors in the prompt, as shown in Table  8.1. These anchors are then used to generate the questions, along with the available  Bloom’s taxonomy templates.

These anchors are then used to generate the questions, along with the available  Bloom’s taxonomy templates. We assume that the anchors will provide a certain  ’closeness’ of important contexts in the course materials. Thus, each course material  (an uploaded document) should have some semantic space acting as ’anchors’ where  all words are ’connected’. The goal of this anchoring method is to ensure that the  generated questions and answers are closely tied to the document’s content, thereby  minimizing OpenAI’s hallucinations (inaccurate or irrelevant responses).

The system prompt in Table 8.1 illustrates context anchoring by utilizing nouns 
extracted from the document to generate relevant questions. These nouns represent 
core information or key concepts. The noun list is included in the prompt to ensure a 
strong relevance between the generated questions and the learning topic. Addition-
ally, the prompt incorporates Bloom’s Taxonomy templates for Level 1 (Remember-
ing) and Level 2 (Understanding), where Remembering emphasizes basic questions 
(e.g., deﬁnitions and facts) and Understanding evaluates students’ ability to interpret 
and compare concepts. 
This anchoring directs the system to generate adaptive questions based on local 
context (key terms from a particular page) while considering global context (key 
terms from the whole document). The process ensures the relevance of questions 
and enhances understanding by broadening coverage based on key terms page by 
page. After generation, nouns from each question are extracted and stored in a list of 
important nouns, i.e. the context anchors for further testing. This method produces 
varied - relevant questions - that link local and global contexts, thereby fostering a 
deeper and adaptive learning experience.

The document is parsed page by page to extract  the text content. A highlighted section introduces the concept of “gradient descent,”  which serves as an anchor for generating learning interactions. After extraction, the system uses TF-IDF analysis for context anchoring to identify  important uni-, bi-, and trigrams. These key terms are then  utilized to generate targeted questions, ensuring the instructional content aligns with  learner prompts. Question generation is guided by Bloom’s taxonomy, using templates such as  “What is…?” or “Why did… happen?” For example, the system automatically creates  the prompt “What is gradient descent?” to promote engagement. Unlike unstructured  generative methods, this template-based approach prevents hallucinations, such as  mixing unrelated concepts like “ridge regression” and “gradient descent,” and keeps  questions grounded in the source material. The observation for context extraction and anchoring started with processing course  material in the form of a PDF ﬁle in English. The material for this evaluation covers  Regularized Linear Models, a chapter from the used textbook [ 15], which spans 20  pages. The English document was translated into Bahasa Indonesia using OpenAI. Additionally, the original English document was also used without translation for  further evaluation. To assess semantic relevance, two remembering and two understanding questions  were created for each page, with extra questions generated based on scores from  low to high. Using the ada-002 model, embeddings were computed from questions,  answers, and page text for both English and Indonesian versions. Cosine similarity  was then employed to measure the semantic closeness between questions, answers,  and their corresponding page content, allowing a bilingual evaluation of contextual  alignment. The analysis results showed that in the Indonesian document, mostly the cosine  similarity values for questions were above 0.85, indicating a high semantic relevance  with the content of the translated document. The highest value reached 0.89, indicat- ing a very high semantic alignment. However, the lowest similarity value was 0.76,  which was caused by a language mismatch. In some cases, questions were written in  English, such as What happens when the hyperparameter .alpha value is set to 0 in  Ridge Regression? The word ’hyperparameter’ should be written as hiperparameter  when translated into Indonesian. This mismatch resulted in a lower cosine similarity values because text embed- ding could not fully capture cross-lingual semantic relevance (Fig. 8.5). Similar issues  were also found in the answers, where answers that were not entirely written in the  same language as the translated document tended to have lower similarity values.

Nevertheless, the Pearson correlation between question similarity and answer simi- larity showed a value of 0.76, indicating a fairly strong relationship. This means that 8 An LLM-Based Adaptive Learning System for Automated Essay … 137 Fig. 8.5 Performance test results of OpenAI with questions and answers in Indonesian  when the question similarity score is high, the answer similarity score also tends to be  high, suggesting that both follow a consistent relevance pattern with the document. The original English document showed higher and more stable semantic similarity  scores, mostly above 0.85 and peaking at 0.92, compared to the translated version. This indicates a stronger alignment between questions, answers, and source text (Fig.  8.6). Despite this, both versions had a similar Pearson correlation (0.76) between  question and answer similarity, indicating consistent relational patterns across lan- guages. These results emphasize the beneﬁt of language consistency in improving  embedding-based semantic evaluations.

Our context anchoring observation shows that—comparing between the global (full 
document) and local (page-level) contexts—the TF-IDF-based anchoring (left graph 
in Fig. 8.7) yields stable cosine similarity scores in both scenarios. Dynamic page-
level anchoring (middle graph in Fig. 8.7) demonstrates greater local consistency but 
presents a signiﬁcant decline in global relevance. Unanchored prompts (right graph 
in Fig. 
8.7) reveal inconsistent cosine similarity scores with broader dispersion. 
Therefore, the global anchoring controlled by the TF-IDF weights has been shown 
to be the most stable and precise approach for generating (prompting) contextually 
relevant questions, as described in Table 8.1.

The TAM evaluation occurred in two phases to ensure the accuracy of the evaluation 
results. In the ﬁrst phase, technical issues arose while running the website, causing 
some respondents to provide feedback based only on a demonstration presented by 
the lecturer. This limited the ability to obtain more in-depth feedback on the user 
experience. In the second phase, the system was fully functional, and all respon-
dents had the opportunity to try it directly. During this phase, they completed a more 
detailed questionnaire designed to gather speciﬁc feedback regarding the user inter-
face, functionality, and their overall experience using the system. A more detailed 
explanation of this phase is provided in the following subsections.

The initial assessment measured PU and PEU using an adapted TAM questionnaire  for chatbot-based learning systems [ 6]. Conducted on November 27, 2024, at Toyo  University, it involved 41 Advanced Multimedia students working with a generative  AI-themed document content in Japanese. Students selected a preferred language  (Japanese, English, or Indonesian), studied a PDF-based lesson, and responded to  AI-generated questions, with additional questions provided if they did not reach the  70% threshold. After the session, participants completed a TAM survey assessing PU, PEU,  risk perception (R), and privacy/security concerns (KP). The system was consid- ered effective if it supported generative AI learning and was seen as accessible and  easy to use. The study also aimed to identify challenges such as missing key concepts  or discomfort during interaction, and examined how background variables and prior  AI experience affected overall technology acceptance (Table  8.2). The evaluation showed a strong correlation (0.991) between PEU and PU, high- lighting the importance of usability in shaping users’ perceptions of system value  (Fig. 8.8). Among PEU indicators, ease of access (PEU2) and understanding ques- tions (PEU1) had the largest contributions, while comfort in system interaction  (PEU3) was less inﬂuential. On the PU side, delivering key concepts (PU3) and  assessment accuracy (PU7) were the most signiﬁcant factors, whereas understand- ing documents (PU1) contributed the least. These ﬁndings suggest that functional  clarity and feedback accuracy are more crucial to user acceptance than comfort or  overall content comprehension. These ﬁndings also imply that, to enhance PEU, the system should ensure bet- ter accessibility (PEU2) and present easily understandable questions (PEU1). To  improve PU, the system should highlight its ability to deliver key concepts (PU3) and  provide accurate assessments (PU7).

To  improve PU, the system should highlight its ability to deliver key concepts (PU3) and  provide accurate assessments (PU7). Enhancing comfort in system interactions could  involve redesigning the interface or chatbot responses (PEU3). Additionally, the  system’s ability to aid in understanding documents (PU1) needs to be strengthened. 140 An LLM-Based Adaptive Learning System... The second evaluation phase occurred in a Machine Learning course at Maranatha  Christian University during the winter semester of 2024/2025 academic year. Stu- dents answered questions based on Chapters 5 (Support V ector Machines) and 6  (Decision Trees) from the course textbook [ 15]. Between April 3 and 7, 2025, 46  students independently tested the system using the questions listed in Table 8.3, with  44 achieving the 70% threshold on their ﬁrst attempt and two on their second. The success threshold was set at 70%. Each student received one question from a  pool of three. If they did not meet the threshold on the ﬁrst question, the subsequent  questions would be presented one at a time. If they still did not succeed after using  all available questions, a ﬁnal question was generated by OpenAI. In this phase (see  Fig.  8.9), the system had been improved based on feedback from the ﬁrst phase. The  correlation between PEU and PU remained strong at 0.850, indicating that the easier  a system is to use, the more beneﬁcial it feels to users. In the improved second phase, the system used an adaptive questioning approach  with a 70% success threshold, offering up to three predeﬁned questions and a ﬁnal  OpenAI-generated fallback if needed (Fig.  8.9). The correlation between PEU and  PU remained strong at 0.850, reinforcing that ease of use increases perceived value. Top PEU contributors included ease of understanding questions (0.710) and inter- face accessibility (0.608), while identifying AI-generated questions scored lowest  (0.415), indicating a need for clearer labels. On the PU side, automatic feedback  (0.837), learning efﬁciency (0.796), and accurate assessments (0.750) were the most  inﬂuential, whereas keyword provision (0.462) was the least impactful, pointing to  potential areas for future improvement, especially in supporting user-driven topic  selection. A comparative analysis reveals signiﬁcant improvements in system effectiveness 
between the two phases. Initially, only 5 out of 21 participants scored above 70%,

The integration of AI into web-based learning platforms offers substantial beneﬁts for  scalable education. The proposed system employs LLM to automate question gener- ation and evaluation, enhancing instructional efﬁciency and reinforcing foundational  learning through alignment with Bloom’s Taxonomy. Evaluation results show that  Fig. 8.9 Second phase TAM analysis results 144 An LLM-Based Adaptive Learning System... the system maintains student engagement and provides timely, automated feedback,  to support comprehension. Despite its strengths, the system faces challenges related to the variability of  LLM-generated outputs, particularly in maintaining consistent question structure. Moreover, its current design is limited in addressing higher-order cognitive tasks  such as analysis and synthesis. Future improvements will focus on reﬁning context- anchoring methods, improving cross-language translation accuracy, and adding col- laborative learning features. These developments aim to advance the system into a  more adaptive and personalized learning solution for diverse educational contexts.  8.6 Implication, Limitation, and Future Work  Experimental results demonstrate the potential of using LLMs to boost student  engagement through self-learning. Starting class sessions with automated online  tutoring could help, allowing instructors to focus on material they ﬁnd difﬁcult during  in-person classes. University policymakers could also more easily monitor learning  progress with outcome-based education. From an ethical perspective, students should be encouraged to critically evaluate  outputs from LLMs. The system presented enables learners to see AI-generated  content in action while highlighting the importance of assessing its accuracy. By  answering AI-generated questions with textbooks or relevant sources, students build  judgment and are guided to operate within academically appropriate limits.

Enhancing  answer evaluation–using metrics like BLEU, ROUGE, or logic-based (qualitative)  scoring–would enable more thorough assessment of complex responses. Additional  features such as visualizations of student performance and personalized feedback  would help instructors track progress and tailor instruction. To support scalability and wider adoption, the system should be tested on vari- ous devices and networks. Adding interactive features like discussion forums and  instructor-reviewed grading is suggested. Improving backend infrastructure and secu- rity, expanding multilingual support, and comparing performance with models like  Claude or Gemini can further boost accuracy and content relevance, especially in  translated or non-native language situations.
